report:
Your skepticism is well-supported by the evidence.

**Conclusion: The claim that soursop "cures cancer" in humans is false — or at minimum, unproven and misleading.**

**What the evidence shows:**

Laboratory (in vitro/animal) studies have found that compounds in soursop, particularly acetogenins like annonacin, show cytotoxic effects against cancer cells in petri dishes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)). This lab-level activity is the basis for widespread claims that soursop is a "natural chemotherapy" or cancer cure.

However, no rigorous human clinical trials have tested soursop as a cancer treatment. As PolitiFact notes, "there haven't been human studies, so we don't know whether it can work as a cancer treatment or not" ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/)). Major cancer institutions agree: Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center and Cancer Research UK both state that soursop's cancer-treatment claims are not supported by reliable clinical evidence, and warn that predatory websites promote graviola capsules as unproven cures ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)).

Fact-checkers at Snopes similarly conclude that while lab chemicals show "potential anticancer properties," there's no evidence supporting soursop as an actual cancer "cure" ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/)).

**Additional concern — safety:** Soursop contains annonacin, a neurotoxin linked in research to atypical Parkinson's disease, particularly in populations with heavy consumption (e.g., Guadeloupe) ([PubMed/Wikipedia on annonacin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)). This makes self-treating cancer with soursop not just ineffective but potentially harmful.

**Bottom line:** The claim conflates preliminary lab findings with proven human efficacy — a common pattern in health misinformation. Soursop is not a validated cancer cure.
